newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil minister linked to cash-for-votes scandal.
newsitem.headline: Brazil minister linked to cash-for-votes scandal.

text.p: A Brazilian corruption scandal deepened on Wednesday when a newspaper linked a government minister to a cash-for-votes scam involving a bill that would allow President Fernando Henrique Cardoso to seek re-election.

The newspaper Folha de Sao Paulo, which alleged on Tuesday that five lawmakers had taken bribes to vote in favour of the bill, said it had new tapes of telephone conversations that suggested Communications Minister Sergio Motta was involved.

Motta's name and his nickname, Serjao, appeared several times in a transcript of the purported conversations which involve two lawmakers talking on separate occasions to an unidentified third person, Folha said.

The newspaper quoted Joao Maia, a federal deputy in Brazil's Congress, as saying Motta had given money to the governor of Amazonas state, Amazonino Mendes, who paid him 200,000 reais ($188,000) for his vote.
"As far as I know it's like this. It was the 200 from Serjao via Amazonino that was the federal contribution to the agreement," Maia was quoted as saying.
A Communications Ministry spokesman said Motta, a close friend of Cardoso, would issue a statement later Wednesday.

The Chamber of Deputies, the lower house of Congress, approved in January a constitutionl amendment that would allow Brazilian presidents, state governors and mayors to run for a second consecutive term. The bill advanced to the Senate where it was due to be put to a vote in a committee on Wednesday.

Cardoso, who hopes to be re-elected as president next year, cast doubt on the authenticity of the allegations. The deputies who were being quoted by Folha de Sao Paulo were "low-level people who don't have credibility," the president said in an interview with national Radio Eldorado.
He called on Congress to investigate quickly the allegations which, he said, took him by surprise.
"I followed the events with the same perplexity as the public," Cardoso told national Radio Eldorado. "If the allegations are proved, immediate steps must be taken."

An internal congressional inquiry was launched on Tuesday and has seven days to investigate the allegations. The probe could lead to suspension of the lawmakers involved in the alleged scam, officials said.

Members of left-wing opposition parties said they would continue gathering signatures for a petition that would set up a wide-ranging Commission of Parliamentary Inquiry (CPI) into the scandal. They also demanded the re-election bill be put on hold.
"It is clear that the whole re-election bill is tainted by these allegations which must be looked into before there are any further votes," said Workers Party deputy Chico Vigilante.

A CPI in the Senate is currently investigating an alleged, multimillion dollar scam involving municipal bonds, one of a string of corruption scandals to rock Congress since former President Fernando Collor stepped down in disgrace in 1992.
